title: Why New Orleans had few local record entrepreneurs
summary: Local people recorded for love of the music or friendship, unlike outsiders such as Chudd and Rupe who came for profit.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: What was... But that gets me back to another question. We have all these people coming in from out of town. Why wouldn't there more... I'm talking in the late 40s, early 50s. Why wouldn't there more entrepreneurs here in New Orleans starting record companies? There would be later on. Yeah.
I don't know. A couple of people tried little things.
Why did they take Lou Chudden and Art Rupp and...

Well, they were, quote, entrepreneurs. They... You see, if a guy down here would have recorded something, he wouldn't have been recording it because this was his chance to make a million dollars. He'd be recording because this guy he heard in a club was so good. I mean, this guy's got to get a break. I'm going to come up with some money and record him and hope...
You know? So it was the... Yeah.
I think people who did it down here at first, at least, did it for the love of the music or the friendship of the player. You know, we didn't have people who were in it purely as...
To make a buck. To make a buck. You think... These other guys.
Rupp. No, yeah. And Lou Chudden and those people.
